svg.title: MAC flooding turns a switch into a hub, and port security is the counter - with three violation behaviours and two practical traps
svg.desc: Left: the three-step mechanism. One, the attacker sends frames with random source MAC addresses at a high rate. Two, the CAM table fills and the real entries age out, so the switch no longer knows which port owns which address. Three, every unknown unicast is flooded to every port in the VLAN, which is exactly what a hub does, and the attacker captures the whole VLAN. Middle: port security as configured - switchport port-security, a maximum of two addresses for one phone plus one PC, a violation behaviour and an aging time. Right: the three violation behaviours compared - protect drops silently with no log and should not be used, restrict drops and raises an SNMP or syslog event and is the recommended default, shutdown err-disables the port which suits high-security zones but costs a manual recovery each time. Bottom: two traps. Setting the maximum too low breaks users who swap docks or plug in a phone plus a PC, and random MAC addresses on modern laptops change the count by themselves. And once 802.1X exists, admission control already covers the main flooding scenario, so port security is mainly a device-count limit and the two must agree on order and on the voice VLAN whitelist.
svg.text: MAC flooding: make the switch forget, and it behaves like a hub
No exploit is involved - the CAM table is a finite resource, and unknown unicast is flooded by design
Frames with random source MACs, sent fast enough that aging cannot keep up
Every frame for an address the switch no longer knows goes to every port in
VLAN 20 - including the attacker's. That is a hub, implemented accidentally.
switchport port-security maximum 2 ! one phone + one PC
silent drop, no log, no counter you watch
almost never - you cannot detect it
drop plus SNMP trap / syslog, port stays up
the default choice for user ports
err-disable the port until someone clears it
Choose by asking who is awake at 02:00: restrict produces a log line,
shutdown produces a support call. Both stop the attack; only one stops the business.
TWO TRAPS THAT SHOW UP IN EVERY REAL DEPLOYMENT

g.text: Users swap USB-C docks, move cables and plug an IP phone plus a PC into
one port. Worse, Windows, macOS and iOS enable random MAC addresses by
default, so the count changes without the user doing anything at all.
Once admission control exists, "no port access before authentication"
already covers the flooding scenario. What port security still adds is a
device count per port - so keep the two consistent on order and voice VLAN.

svg.text: Design note: the CAM table is per-VLAN and per-line-card. On a large stack the symptom of flooding is not "one port is odd" but "sudden broadcast-like load everywhere in one VLAN".
